source.name: OER Commons open behavioral finance curriculum

course.title: Behavioral Finance
course.description: Why real investors are not the cool calculators that textbook theory assumes. This course tours the psychology behind money decisions — prospect theory, mental accounting, the classic heuristics and biases, herding, framing, and the design of better choices — and hands you tools to spot and fight your own mistakes. Structure adapted from open behavioral-finance curricula on OER Commons (CC BY 4.0); all explanations original.

questions.prompt: Standard finance theory assumes investors are…
options: rational agents who maximize expected utility
questions.explanation: The classical model assumes rational, self-interested agents — behavioral finance studies where real people depart from it. See 'Rational vs. real investors'.

questions.prompt: Prospect theory says people feel a loss…
options: exactly as strongly as an equal gain
more strongly than an equal gain
less strongly than an equal gain
only when it is very large
questions.explanation: Losses loom larger than gains — the core idea of loss aversion. See 'Prospect theory and loss aversion'.

questions.prompt: Treating a tax refund as 'fun money' while guarding your salary carefully is an example of…
questions.explanation: Money is treated differently by its imagined 'account,' even though a dollar is a dollar. See 'Mental accounting'.

questions.prompt: Estimating a probability by how easily examples come to mind is the…
questions.explanation: Availability substitutes ease of recall for true frequency. See 'Heuristics and biases'.

questions.prompt: The tendency to hold losing investments too long and sell winners too soon is called…
questions.explanation: The disposition effect follows directly from loss aversion applied to a portfolio. See 'The disposition effect'.

questions.prompt: Automatically enrolling employees in a retirement plan, while letting them opt out, is an example of…
questions.explanation: Changing the default is choice architecture — a nudge that preserves freedom to opt out. See 'Nudges and choice architecture'.

questions.prompt: A 'bias' in this course means…
options: a systematic, predictable error in judgment
questions.explanation: Biases are systematic and repeatable, which is what makes them studyable and correctable.

questions.prompt: Which statement best fits the efficient-market view that behavioral finance pushes back on?
options: Prices often stay wrong for years
Prices already reflect all available information
questions.explanation: The efficient-market hypothesis says prices fully reflect information; anomalies are the cracks behavioral finance points to. See 'Market anomalies'.

lessons.title: Rational vs. real investors
lessons.grammar_note: Keep two labels straight: the idealized 'rational agent' of theory versus the flesh-and-blood investor studied here. Behavioral finance is the study of the gap between them.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Contrast the rational-agent model of standard finance with how people actually decide, and name the three assumptions behavioral finance relaxes. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, what does standard theory assume investors are trying to maximize?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Classical finance builds on a tidy actor sometimes called 'homo economicus': someone with stable, consistent preferences who processes all available information and chooses the option with the highest expected utility. That model relaxes into three testable assumptions — perfect rationality (no logical errors), perfect self-interest (only your own payoff matters), and perfect information use (you weigh every relevant fact correctly). Behavioral finance does not throw the model away; it asks where real people systematically break each assumption. People show bounded rationality (limited attention and mental shortcuts), bounded self-interest (fairness and reciprocity matter), and bounded willpower (they act against their own long-run plans). The word that ties the field together is 'systematic' — the errors are not random noise that averages out, but predictable patterns you can anticipate.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Bounded rationality: asked whether more English words start with 'r' or have 'r' as the third letter, most people say the first, because leading-letter words are easier to recall — even though third-position words are far more common. Bounded self-interest: in the ultimatum game, one player splits ten dollars and the other can accept or reject; a purely self-interested responder would take any positive offer, yet real responders routinely reject offers below about three dollars to punish unfairness. Bounded willpower: a saver fully intends to add to a retirement account each month, then repeatedly spends the money instead — the plan and the action diverge.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Name the three assumptions of the rational-agent model. 2) Which assumption is violated when someone rejects a 'take it or leave it' one-dollar offer out of ten? 3) Is a coin-flip forecasting error that averages to zero a 'bias' in this course's sense? 4) Give one everyday example of bounded willpower. 5) True or false: behavioral finance claims people are simply stupid. Answers: 1) perfect rationality, perfect self-interest, and perfect information use. 2) bounded self-interest (fairness overrides pure payoff). 3) No — a bias must be systematic, not random noise. 4) e.g. planning to diet then ordering dessert; planning to save then overspending. 5) False — it maps predictable patterns in normal, intelligent people.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: assuming behavioral finance says markets are always wrong — it says people are predictably imperfect, which sometimes but not always moves prices. Mistake: calling any single bad outcome a 'bias'; a bias is a repeatable tendency, visible across many people and trials. Exit: (a) What single word distinguishes a bias from ordinary noise? (b) Name one of the three 'bounded' limits on the rational actor. Answers: systematic; bounded rationality, bounded self-interest, or bounded willpower.

lessons.title: Prospect theory and loss aversion
lessons.grammar_note: In prospect theory, outcomes are judged as gains or losses relative to a reference point, not as final wealth levels. Change the reference point and the same outcome can flip from a gain to a loss.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: State the three pillars of prospect theory — reference dependence, diminishing sensitivity, and loss aversion — and use them to predict risk-taking. Warm-up: would losing fifty dollars or gaining fifty dollars change your mood more?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Prospect theory, the descriptive alternative to expected-utility theory, rests on three pillars. First, reference dependence: people evaluate outcomes as gains or losses measured from a reference point (often the status quo or a purchase price), not as absolute wealth. Second, diminishing sensitivity: the difference between 10 and 20 dollars feels bigger than the difference between 1010 and 1020, so the value curve is concave for gains and convex for losses. Third, loss aversion: the pain of a loss is roughly twice the pleasure of an equal gain, so the curve is steeper on the loss side. A direct consequence is a predictable flip in risk attitude — people tend to be risk-averse when facing gains (they lock in a sure win) but risk-seeking when facing losses (they gamble to avoid a sure loss).

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: The reflection effect: offered a sure 500 dollars versus a fifty-fifty shot at 1000, most take the sure 500 — risk-averse over gains. Now offered a sure loss of 500 versus a fifty-fifty shot at losing 1000 or nothing, most gamble — risk-seeking over losses, trying to escape the certain loss. The endowment effect follows from loss aversion: give people a mug and they demand about twice as much to sell it as buyers will pay, because giving it up registers as a loss. A rough loss-aversion coefficient: if losing 100 dollars hurts as much as gaining 200 dollars pleases, the ratio is about 2 to 1.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Name the three pillars of prospect theory. 2) A stock you bought at 40 now trades at 30; against what reference point are you feeling a loss? 3) Are people typically risk-seeking or risk-averse when all options are losses? 4) If losing 50 dollars feels about as intense as gaining 100, what is the approximate loss-aversion ratio? 5) The endowment effect makes owners value a good more than buyers — which pillar explains it? Answers: 1) reference dependence, diminishing sensitivity, and loss aversion. 2) the 40 purchase price. 3) risk-seeking (they gamble to avoid a certain loss). 4) about 2 to 1. 5) loss aversion (parting with it registers as a loss).

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: describing loss aversion as 'people dislike losing money' in general — the precise claim is that a loss hurts more than an equal gain pleases. Mistake: forgetting that the reference point is chosen, not fixed; reframing the baseline can turn a felt loss into a felt gain. Exit: (a) Roughly how many times stronger is a loss than an equal gain? (b) Over losses, are people risk-averse or risk-seeking? Answers: about twice; risk-seeking.

lessons.title: Mental accounting
lessons.grammar_note: Money is 'fungible' — any dollar can substitute for any other. Mental accounting is the habit of treating dollars as if they were not fungible, tagging them by source or purpose.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Define mental accounting and identify how source, labeling, and separate 'buckets' distort spending and investing. Warm-up: would you spend a surprise 100-dollar lottery win more freely than 100 dollars from your paycheck?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Mental accounting is the tendency to sort money into separate psychological accounts and treat each differently, even though economically a dollar is a dollar — it is fully fungible. People tag money by its source (windfalls feel spendable; hard-earned salary feels protected), by its intended purpose (a 'vacation fund' is guarded even while credit-card debt grows), and by separate mental buckets that are never netted against each other. This produces clear errors: paying 18 percent interest on a card while keeping cash in a 1 percent savings jar; treating 'house money' from an early win as free to gamble; or feeling that a 5-dollar saving on a 15-dollar item is worth a trip across town, but the same 5 dollars off a 500-dollar item is not — the saving is judged relative to its account, not on its own.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Windfall spending: people blow a tax refund on a treat but would never pull the identical sum from savings, because the refund is filed in a 'bonus' account. House money: after an early gambling win, players take bigger risks with 'the casino's money,' forgetting it is now theirs. The debt paradox: a household keeps 2000 dollars in a savings account earning almost nothing while carrying a 2000-dollar card balance at 18 percent — netting the buckets would save hundreds a year. Relative framing: shoppers drive twenty minutes to save 5 dollars on a 15-dollar calculator but not to save the same 5 dollars on a 500-dollar laptop, though the twenty minutes is worth the same either way.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) What property of money does mental accounting ignore? 2) Why might someone keep a 'vacation fund' while running a credit-card balance? 3) In the 'house money' effect, whose money are gamblers actually risking after a win? 4) Is a 5-dollar saving worth more on a cheap item or an expensive one, economically? 5) Name one real cost of splitting money into rigid buckets. Answers: 1) fungibility (a dollar is a dollar). 2) the two buckets are never netted, so the guarded fund and the costly debt coexist. 3) their own — the winnings are theirs the moment they are won. 4) the same — five dollars is five dollars regardless of the item's price. 5) e.g. paying high interest while cash sits idle, or under- or over-spending a labeled account.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: assuming mental accounting is always harmful — labeled buckets can aid self-control, as with a dedicated emergency fund; the error is refusing to net accounts when it clearly costs money. Mistake: thinking windfalls are objectively different money; they spend exactly like any other dollar. Exit: (a) What single word names the property mental accounting overlooks? (b) Give one situation where splitting money into buckets helps rather than hurts. Answers: fungibility; e.g. an earmarked emergency or retirement fund that protects long-run goals.

questions.prompt: Behavioral finance mainly studies…
options: systematic gaps between rational theory and real behavior
questions.explanation: The field maps predictable, systematic departures from the rational-agent model. See 'Rational vs. real investors'.

questions.prompt: In prospect theory, outcomes are evaluated relative to…
questions.explanation: Reference dependence is the first pillar — gains and losses are measured from a baseline.

questions.prompt: Loss aversion means a loss feels, compared with an equal gain, about…
questions.explanation: The pain of a loss is roughly twice the pleasure of a matching gain.

questions.prompt: When all choices are framed as losses, people tend to become…
questions.explanation: The reflection effect: people gamble to avoid a certain loss.

questions.prompt: Keeping cash in low-interest savings while carrying high-interest card debt is a failure to respect money's…
questions.explanation: The two mental buckets are never netted, though a dollar is a dollar.

questions.prompt: The endowment effect — owners demanding more to sell than buyers will pay — is explained by…
questions.explanation: Giving up the owned item registers as a loss, which looms larger.

lessons.title: Heuristics and biases: anchoring, availability, overconfidence
lessons.grammar_note: A heuristic is a mental shortcut — usually helpful. A bias is the systematic error a heuristic produces when it misfires. Same mechanism, two names depending on the outcome.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Define three workhorse heuristics — anchoring, availability, and overconfidence — and spot each in a financial setting. Warm-up: if I first ask whether a stock will pass 200 dollars, does that number color your own price guess?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: The mind economizes with heuristics, fast rules of thumb that usually work but fail in patterned ways. Anchoring: an initial number, even an irrelevant one, pulls later estimates toward it; people adjust away from the anchor but stop too soon. Availability: we judge how likely something is by how easily examples come to mind, so vivid, recent, or heavily reported events feel more probable than they are. Overconfidence has three faces — overestimation (thinking you are better than you are), overplacement (thinking you beat most others, the 'better than average' effect), and overprecision (confidence intervals that are far too narrow). In markets these produce anchored valuations, panic driven by recent headlines, and excessive trading by investors sure they can beat the average.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Anchoring: people who first wrote down the last two digits of an ID number then bid more for a bottle of wine when those digits were high — an obviously irrelevant anchor still moved the price. In investing, a stock's 52-week high becomes an anchor that makes today's price look 'cheap.' Availability: after heavy coverage of a plane crash, travelers overestimate flight risk and drive instead, though driving is far more dangerous per mile; likewise a recent market crash makes investors overweight the odds of the next one. Overconfidence: asked for a 90 percent confidence range for the length of the Nile, most people give a range that misses the true value — overprecision. In one classic study the most active (most overconfident) traders earned the lowest net returns after costs.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Which heuristic explains treating a stock's past high as a reference for 'cheap'? 2) Why do sensational news events feel more probable than dull, common ones? 3) Name the three forms of overconfidence. 4) A negotiator opens with a high price to shift the final deal upward — which effect is used? 5) Overprecision shows up as confidence intervals that are too what? Answers: 1) anchoring. 2) availability — they are easier to recall. 3) overestimation, overplacement, and overprecision. 4) anchoring. 5) too narrow.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: calling heuristics simply 'bad thinking' — they are efficient shortcuts that are right often enough to be worth using; the bias is the predictable miss. Mistake: confusing overplacement ('I beat most people') with overprecision ('my range is too tight') — they are different failures. Exit: (a) Which heuristic makes an arbitrary starting number distort an estimate? (b) Which form of overconfidence is the 'better than average' effect? Answers: anchoring; overplacement.

lessons.title: Herding and bubbles
lessons.grammar_note: Distinguish a 'bubble' — price far above fundamental value driven by expectations of further rises — from ordinary volatility. A bubble is defined by the gap from fundamentals, not merely by a big move.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain why individually reasonable people herd, and trace the anatomy of a speculative bubble from boom to bust. Warm-up: if everyone you know is buying an asset, what non-financial pressure pushes you to join?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Herding is the tendency to copy the crowd rather than act on private information. It can even be individually rational: in an information cascade, each person infers that the crowd must know something and discounts their own signal, so private information stops entering prices. Reputational herding adds a career motive — it is safer to be wrong alongside everyone than to be wrong alone. When herding meets easy credit and a compelling story, prices can detach from fundamental value, producing a bubble. A common arc runs displacement (a new technology or story), boom (rising prices draw in more buyers), euphoria ('this time is different,' valuations ignored), profit-taking by insiders, and finally panic as the crowd reverses at once. Limits to arbitrage explain why smart money often cannot simply short a bubble away: staying solvent while a bubble inflates can be impossible.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Information cascade: diners pick the busier of two empty-looking restaurants, each assuming the early customers knew best, so a full room can result from almost no real information. Tulip mania in the 1630s, the South Sea Bubble of 1720, the late-1990s dot-com boom, and the mid-2000s housing bubble share the same arc — a story, leverage, euphoric valuations, then a fast collapse. Limits to arbitrage: a trader who correctly judged tech stocks overpriced in 1998 and shorted them could have been wiped out well before the 2000 peak, because 'the market can stay irrational longer than you can stay solvent.'

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) In an information cascade, what do people stop doing with their own private signal? 2) Give the one-word career reason people herd even when doubtful. 3) List the typical stages of a bubble in order. 4) What defines a bubble beyond just a large price move? 5) Why can't rational traders always short a bubble to death? Answers: 1) they ignore or discount it, inferring the crowd knows more. 2) reputation (safer to be wrong with everyone). 3) displacement, boom, euphoria, profit-taking, panic. 4) a wide gap between price and fundamental value. 5) limits to arbitrage — they can run out of capital before prices correct.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: assuming herding is always irrational — following the crowd can be a sensible inference when others may be better informed; the danger is that private information stops feeding the price. Mistake: labeling every sharp drop a 'burst bubble'; a bubble requires prior detachment from fundamentals. Exit: (a) What term describes each person copying the crowd and shelving their own signal? (b) Name the phrase capturing why shorting a bubble is dangerous. Answers: an information cascade; markets can stay irrational longer than you can stay solvent (limits to arbitrage).

lessons.title: Framing and the disposition effect
lessons.grammar_note: 'Framing' is how a choice is described; 'the disposition effect' is a specific trading pattern. The lesson pairs them because the disposition effect is loss aversion working on a frame — the purchase price.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Show how logically identical options change behavior when reframed, and explain the disposition effect as loss aversion anchored to purchase price. Warm-up: does '90 percent survival' sound better than '10 percent mortality,' even though they are the same?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Framing is the finding that the way a choice is worded — not just its content — changes the decision. A gain frame and a loss frame describing the identical outcome can flip people between caution and gambling, because each frame moves the reference point of prospect theory. The disposition effect is a market fingerprint of this: investors sell winners too early and hold losers too long. The mechanism is loss aversion measured against the purchase price. A stock above what you paid sits in the 'gain' region, where you are risk-averse and want to lock in the win; a stock below your cost sits in the 'loss' region, where you turn risk-seeking and gamble on a rebound rather than realize the loss. The result is systematically worse than the reverse — for tax reasons alone, realizing losses and deferring gains would usually be smarter.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Framing (the classic disease problem): a program that 'saves 200 of 600 people' is chosen over an equivalent gamble, but when the same math is framed as '400 will die,' people flip to the gamble — identical outcomes, opposite choices. Attribute framing: ground beef labeled '80 percent lean' outsells the same product labeled '20 percent fat.' The disposition effect: an investor bought Stock A and Stock B at 50; A rises to 70 and B falls to 30, and needing cash the investor sells A (banking the gain) while clinging to B hoping it returns to 50 — the reverse of what taxes and momentum evidence would suggest.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Are '90 percent survival' and '10 percent mortality' logically the same? 2) In the disposition effect, which does the investor sell too soon — winners or losers? 3) Against what reference point is a holding judged a gain or loss? 4) Why is holding losers and dumping winners often tax-inefficient? 5) Reframing '400 will die' as '200 will be saved' shifts people toward which attitude? Answers: 1) yes, exactly the same. 2) winners. 3) the purchase price. 4) realizing losses can reduce taxes while realizing gains creates a tax bill, so the common pattern is backwards. 5) toward risk-aversion (choosing the sure option).

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: thinking framing only fools careless people — it moves experts, including physicians, because it shifts the reference point everyone reasons from. Mistake: describing the disposition effect as 'selling losers' — it is the opposite, clinging to losers and cashing out winners. Exit: (a) The disposition effect makes investors hold which category too long? (b) What single anchor turns a holding into a felt gain or loss? Answers: losers; the purchase price.

questions.prompt: Letting an arbitrary starting number distort a later estimate is…
questions.explanation: Anchoring pulls estimates toward an initial value, even an irrelevant one.

questions.prompt: Overestimating rare, vivid events because they are easy to recall is the…
questions.explanation: Availability substitutes ease of recall for true frequency.

questions.prompt: The 'better than average' belief that you beat most other people is a form of overconfidence called…
questions.explanation: Overplacement is misjudging your rank relative to others.

questions.prompt: In an information cascade, individuals…
options: discount their own signal and copy the crowd
questions.explanation: Each infers the crowd is informed, so private signals stop entering prices.

questions.prompt: The disposition effect describes investors who…
options: sell winners too early and hold losers too long
sell losers too early and hold winners too long
questions.explanation: Loss aversion against the purchase price drives cashing gains and clinging to losses.

questions.prompt: Ground beef sells better as '80 percent lean' than '20 percent fat.' This is…
questions.explanation: The same fact, differently worded, changes the choice — attribute framing.

lessons.title: Nudges and choice architecture
lessons.grammar_note: A 'nudge' changes behavior without removing options or changing incentives much; a 'mandate' removes options. If someone can easily opt out, it is a nudge, not a mandate.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Define a nudge, explain why defaults are so powerful, and design one to improve a financial decision. Warm-up: if a retirement plan enrolled you automatically but let you quit anytime, would you stay in?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Choice architecture is the observation that how options are arranged — the order, the default, the number of choices — inevitably shapes decisions, so there is no 'neutral' design. A nudge is any feature of that architecture that predictably steers behavior while preserving freedom of choice and leaving incentives largely intact. Defaults are the strongest lever, for three reasons: inertia (staying put is easy), implied endorsement (the default reads as a recommendation), and loss aversion (leaving the default can feel like giving something up). Because people follow the path of least resistance, setting a helpful default — automatic enrollment, automatic escalation of savings, sensible fund choices — moves far more behavior than exhortation. Good nudges also simplify: fewer, clearer options reduce the paralysis that too much choice creates.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Automatic enrollment: switching a retirement plan from opt-in to opt-out has pushed participation from roughly half to over ninety percent, because most people accept whatever the default is. Automatic escalation ('Save More Tomorrow') raises the contribution rate at each future raise, sidestepping the pain of a pay cut today. Organ-donation rates are dramatically higher in opt-out countries than nearly identical opt-in neighbors — the default, not deep preference, drives the gap. Simplification: cutting a fund menu from dozens of options to a few well-labeled choices raises enrollment, because too many options trigger paralysis.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) What two things must a nudge preserve to count as a nudge and not a mandate? 2) Name the three reasons defaults are so sticky. 3) Why does 'Save More Tomorrow' schedule increases for the future rather than now? 4) Is banning a product a nudge? 5) How can offering fewer investment options increase participation? Answers: 1) freedom of choice (easy opt-out) and roughly unchanged incentives. 2) inertia, implied endorsement, and loss aversion. 3) to avoid the felt loss of a pay cut today, since the raise cushions it. 4) no — removing an option is a mandate, not a nudge. 5) it reduces choice overload and decision paralysis.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: thinking there can be a 'no-design' default — some option must come first or be preselected, so architecture is unavoidable; the only choice is whether it is thoughtful. Mistake: calling any incentive a nudge; a nudge leaves incentives largely intact and options open. Exit: (a) What is the single most powerful nudge lever? (b) Name one reason defaults stick. Answers: the default option; inertia, implied endorsement, or loss aversion.

lessons.title: Market anomalies
lessons.grammar_note: An 'anomaly' is a return pattern the efficient-market model does not predict. Some survive scrutiny; some fade after discovery or vanish once trading costs are included. Treat each skeptically.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: State the efficient-market hypothesis, describe well-known anomalies, and explain why an anomaly is not a free lunch. Warm-up: if a pattern reliably beat the market, what would happen once everyone traded on it?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: The efficient-market hypothesis (EMH) says prices already reflect available information, so consistently earning risk-adjusted excess returns should be impossible. Anomalies are documented patterns that seem to contradict this. Cross-sectional anomalies compare stocks at one time: the value effect (cheap 'value' stocks historically beat expensive 'growth' stocks) and the size effect (small firms outperformed large ones). Momentum is the tendency of recent winners to keep winning over months — awkward for both EMH and simple behavioral stories. Calendar anomalies like the January effect or turn-of-month patterns are weaker and often fade. Behavioral finance reads many anomalies as the market price of crowd errors — overreaction and underreaction — while defenders of EMH argue the extra return is just compensation for risk, or that the pattern disappears after trading costs. The honest verdict: some anomalies are real and persistent, many shrink once they are published and arbitraged, and none is a guaranteed profit.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Value versus growth: portfolios of low price-to-book stocks historically outran high price-to-book stocks over long horizons, though with stretches of severe underperformance. Momentum: buying the past twelve-month winners and selling the losers earned positive average returns across many markets, yet suffers rare, brutal crashes. Post-earnings-announcement drift: prices keep drifting in the direction of an earnings surprise for weeks, an underreaction the EMH struggles to explain. Fading anomaly: the small-firm 'January effect' weakened markedly after it was widely publicized, illustrating how discovery can erode an edge.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) What does the efficient-market hypothesis claim about prices? 2) Name two cross-sectional anomalies. 3) Momentum favors recent winners or recent losers over the next few months? 4) Give one EMH-friendly explanation for an apparent anomaly. 5) Why might a real anomaly shrink after it is published? Answers: 1) prices already reflect available information, so consistent risk-adjusted excess returns are not possible. 2) the value effect and the size effect (also momentum). 3) recent winners. 4) the extra return is compensation for risk, or it disappears after trading costs. 5) traders exploit it until the mispricing is competed away.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: treating any anomaly as a money machine — after costs, taxes, and the risk of long droughts, most edges are thin or gone. Mistake: assuming every anomaly proves markets are irrational; some are just risk premia in disguise. Exit: (a) What does EMH say prices already reflect? (b) Name one anomaly that tends to persist and one that tends to fade. Answers: available information; momentum or value tends to persist, while the January effect tends to fade.

lessons.title: Debiasing strategies
lessons.grammar_note: Debiasing rarely means 'try harder to be rational.' It usually means changing the environment or the procedure so the bias has less room to act. Design beats willpower.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Match common biases to concrete countermeasures and explain why structural fixes beat sheer effort. Warm-up: which is more reliable for saving money — resolving to save each month, or an automatic transfer on payday?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Because biases are systematic, they can be countered systematically. The strongest tools change the decision environment rather than relying on willpower. Commitment devices lock in a good choice in advance — automatic transfers, restricted accounts, precommitted rules — so bounded willpower has nothing to undo. Checklists and rules force a full, consistent process, blunting availability and overconfidence. Consider-the-opposite and the pre-mortem (imagine the plan has failed and explain why) widen a too-narrow view and puncture overprecision. Reframing in absolute terms (final wealth, base rates) defuses loss-aversion and framing traps. Diversification and rebalancing turn discipline into a mechanical schedule, countering the disposition effect and herding. Cooling-off periods interrupt panic selling driven by vivid recent news. The recurring principle: redesign the choice so the bias cannot easily operate, rather than hoping to out-think it in the moment.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Commitment device: an automatic payday transfer to savings beats a monthly intention, because it removes the willpower step entirely. Pre-mortem: before an acquisition, a team writes 'it is two years later and this failed — why?' and surfaces risks that optimism had hidden. Rebalancing rule: a fixed 'sell what rose, buy what fell back to target weights' schedule forces you to trim winners and add to losers — the discipline the disposition effect erodes. Consider-the-opposite: an analyst bullish on a stock deliberately lists three reasons it could fall, widening an overprecise forecast. Cooling-off: a rule to wait 48 hours before selling on scary headlines curbs availability-driven panic.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Why do structural fixes usually beat 'trying harder'? 2) Name a commitment device for saving. 3) What does a pre-mortem ask you to imagine? 4) Which bias does a scheduled rebalancing rule directly counter? 5) How does a cooling-off period fight availability-driven panic? Answers: 1) biases act automatically, so changing the environment removes the chance to slip rather than relying on scarce willpower. 2) an automatic payday transfer or a restricted savings account. 3) that the plan has already failed, then explain why. 4) the disposition effect (and herding). 5) it delays action past the vivid moment, letting recency fade before deciding.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: believing awareness alone fixes a bias — knowing about anchoring barely reduces it; you need a procedure or a changed environment. Mistake: piling on so many rules that decisions stall; a few well-chosen structural fixes outperform endless vigilance. Exit: (a) What kind of fix generally beats willpower? (b) Name one debiasing tool for overprecision. Answers: a structural or environmental fix (e.g. a commitment device); consider-the-opposite or a pre-mortem.

questions.prompt: A feature that steers behavior while keeping options open and incentives roughly intact is a…
questions.explanation: Preserving free opt-out and incentives is what makes it a nudge. See 'Nudges and choice architecture'.

questions.prompt: The single most powerful nudge is usually the…
questions.explanation: Inertia, implied endorsement, and loss aversion make defaults stick.

questions.prompt: The efficient-market hypothesis claims prices already reflect…
questions.explanation: If information is priced in, consistent risk-adjusted excess returns should be impossible.

questions.prompt: Buying recent winners and selling recent losers exploits which anomaly?
questions.explanation: Momentum is the tendency of recent winners to keep winning over months.

questions.prompt: An automatic payday transfer to savings is best described as a…
questions.explanation: It locks in the good choice ahead of time, removing the willpower step.

questions.prompt: A pre-mortem reduces overprecision by asking a team to imagine that…
questions.explanation: Explaining an imagined failure surfaces risks optimism had hidden.

lessons.title: Capstone: analyze a real decision
lessons.grammar_note: Your job here is diagnosis, not confession. Name the bias, cite the evidence in the story, and prescribe a structural fix — the same three moves you would apply to a client or a company.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Take a real financial decision, diagnose the biases at work, and prescribe concrete debiasing fixes — pulling together every idea in the course. Warm-up: think of one money decision you or someone you know handled badly. Which lesson does it most resemble?

sections.heading: The task
sections.text: Choose one real decision — your own, a friend's, or a documented public case such as a famous bubble or a corporate blunder. Write a short analysis, about 400 to 600 words, in three parts. Part 1, describe the decision plainly: who decided, what they chose, and the outcome. Part 2, diagnose at least three biases from this course, quoting the specific detail in the story that reveals each — do not just name-drop terms. Part 3, prescribe a concrete structural fix for each bias (a default, a rule, a commitment device, a cooling-off period, a pre-mortem), explaining why the fix disarms that particular error. Aim for a diagnosis a classmate could act on, not a vague 'be more rational.'

sections.heading: A fully worked model (a different case)
sections.text: Decision: In 2007 a household bought a home far above their budget with an adjustable-rate mortgage, then defaulted in 2009. Diagnosis: (1) Herding and the availability heuristic — 'everyone was buying and prices only ever went up' shows a crowd cascade plus recent-price extrapolation; the tell is the phrase 'this time is different.' (2) Overconfidence (overprecision) — they assumed they could refinance before the rate reset, a confidence interval far too narrow for future rates; the tell is that they made no plan for the reset. (3) Anchoring and mental accounting — they anchored affordability to the introductory 'teaser' monthly payment rather than the fully reset payment, filing the two payments in separate mental buckets; the tell is budgeting only the low first-year figure. Prescription: for the herding and availability, a rule to value a home on rent-versus-buy fundamentals, not recent price trends; for the overprecision, a pre-mortem ('the rate reset and we cannot refinance — what then?') and a stress test at the maximum possible payment; for the anchoring, a hard rule to budget against the fully reset payment, netting all housing costs into one account. Notice the shape: name the bias, quote the evidence, prescribe a structural fix.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Draft your own three-part analysis now, then self-test with these prompts. 1) Did you name at least three distinct biases, each tied to a specific detail? 2) For each bias, is the tell a concrete quote or fact, not a general impression? 3) Is every prescribed fix structural (a default, rule, commitment device, cooling-off, or pre-mortem) rather than 'try harder'? 4) Could a classmate act on your prescriptions without asking you what you meant? 5) Did you avoid hindsight bias — judging the decision only because you know the outcome — by pointing to errors visible at the time? Answers: a strong capstone answers yes to all five; if any is no, revise that part before moving on.

sections.heading: Self-check rubric & wrap-up
sections.text: Score your analysis: (a) three or more biases correctly named; (b) each backed by a specific detail from the story; (c) a distinct, structural fix for each; (d) fixes that plausibly disarm the bias, not just restate it; (e) reasoning that would have been available before the outcome, avoiding hindsight bias. Five yeses means you can now do the core work of behavioral finance: see the systematic error behind a money decision and redesign the choice so the error has less room to act. That is the whole course in one skill — from the rational-versus-real gap through prospect theory, mental accounting, the heuristics, herding, framing, nudges, and anomalies, all the way to fixing a real decision.

questions.prompt: Behavioral finance differs from classical finance mainly by studying…

questions.explanation: It maps repeatable patterns where real people diverge from the rational-agent model.

hold winners too long and sell losers too soon

questions.explanation: Publication and trading erode edges, and some 'anomalies' are just risk premia.

questions.explanation: Structural fixes such as commitment devices beat sheer willpower.
